To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

DIR and CIR are manifestations of the same underlying mechanism; that CIR is not an alternative to DIR, but rather a special case of DIR; that DIR and CRI are manifestations of the molecular scheme that governs DIR under conditions of depolarization, and that the same scheme governs the spontaneous release under conditions where depolarization and [Ca2+](i) are both absent; and that the estimates of [Ca2+],i under physiological conditions are too high.
DIR and CIR are governed by different molecular schemes, and that the Ca2+-dependent molecular scheme for CIR is a subset of that for DIR.

(1) DIR can be described in terms of a simple molecular scheme; (2) the molecular scheme for release under conditions of depolarization is the same as for spontaneous release, but the molecular scheme is not the same as that for release under conditions where [Ca2+] is high and depolarization is lacking.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the reconciliation of the Ca2+ and the Ca2+voltage hypotheses, which are both correct, and with the clarification of the molecular mechanisms for DIR and CIR, and their relationship to each other.

DIR is initiated by membrane depolarization, which triggers the influx of extracellular Ca2+ into the nerve terminal.
the Ca2+- voltage hypothesis is correct, but the Ca2+ concentrations that are required are much lower than those that have been measured under conditions of C1R.
DIR is a Ca2+-vaccinated depolarization-induced phenomenon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Ca2+-dependent molecular scheme for DIR can be divided into two subsets: one subset is activated by depolarization, whereas the other subset is activated by Ca2+ alone.
the Ca2+ concentration in the physiological DIR is not high enough to trigger spontaneous release, but is high enough to promote DIR by the Ca2+-dependent mechanism.
CIR is not a form of release that is initiated by depolarization, as is DIR.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Ca2+ and Ca2+-village hypotheses for DIR are not mutually exclusive, and that the Ca2+- voltage hypothesis can explain CIR.
DIR and CIR can be viewed as manifestations of a single molecular scheme for neurotransmitter release.
DIR and CIR are two sides of the same coin.
